summary: Generalizes the pseudowire Associated Channel Header so a control channel can be attached to MPLS label switched paths and MPLS sections, not just pseudowires. It also defines how to signal the presence of the header in the label stack, which helps with operations and management messages.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5586 defines a common way to carry maintenance and control messages over MPLS pseudowires, paths and sections. A four-byte Associated Channel Header identifies the message type, and label 13 identifies the header on paths and sections. The RFC defines how to package these messages, not how each maintenance protocol works.

subtitle: A shared control channel for MPLS paths and links, identified by the Generic Associated Channel Label.

tldr.problem: MPLS maintenance messages need a consistent in-band control channel for pseudowires, label switched paths and sections. The existing Associated Channel Header was defined for pseudowires.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5586 generalizes the Associated Channel Header as the Generic Associated Channel. On paths and sections, the reserved Generic Associated Channel Label, value 13, signals that the header follows the bottom of the label stack.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5586 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3032, RFC 4385 and RFC 5085. It defines encapsulation, not channel negotiation or the operation of the maintenance protocols, and has been updated by RFC 6423, RFC 7026, RFC 7214 and RFC 7274.

today: RFC 5586 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3032, RFC 4385 and RFC 5085. It has since been updated by RFC 6423, RFC 7026, RFC 7214 and RFC 7274.

sections.title: A Common Channel for MPLS Maintenance
sections.content:
Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) messages help operators detect faults, diagnose problems and maintain a network. RFC 5586 says these functions should work in much the same way on MPLS pseudowires (PWs), Label Switched Paths (LSPs) and MPLS Sections. They should travel in-band and should not depend on user traffic or dynamic control-plane functions.

The Associated Channel Header (ACH) already carried control messages for pseudowires. RFC 5586 generalizes it as the Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh), so the same channel mechanism can also be used for LSPs and sections. The document defines encapsulation only; it does not define negotiation or the behavior of individual OAM functions.
sections.plainLanguage: Network operators need maintenance messages that can travel with MPLS traffic on different kinds of paths. RFC 5586 provides a shared format for those messages but leaves each maintenance protocol's behavior to its own specification.

sections.title: The Associated Channel Header
sections.content:
The ACH is a 32-bit word. Its first nibble is 0001, which identifies a control channel associated with a pseudowire, LSP or section. The version field is 0. Bits 8 through 15 are reserved, must be zero when sent and are ignored when received.

The final 16 bits are the Channel Type in network byte order. They identify the carried protocol or function, such as IPv4, IPv6 or a maintenance protocol. A specification that defines a protocol using the ACH must also specify its Channel Type. The G-ACh must not carry user traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The header starts with a marker and version, then uses its final field to identify the message type. The receiving router uses that type to select the right processing function.

sections.title: Optional ACH Type-Length-Value Data
sections.content:
Some channel messages need extra context, such as information about the source or intended destination. RFC 5586 allows ACH Type-Length-Value (TLV) data only when the relevant Channel Type specification explicitly permits it. If TLVs are allowed, a four-octet ACH TLV Header must follow the ACH even when that packet contains no TLVs; its length is then zero.

The header's 16-bit Length counts all following TLVs and sub-TLVs, and its 16-bit Reserved field is set to zero. Each TLV has a 16-bit Type, a 16-bit length for its value, and the value itself. No padding is required.
sections.plainLanguage: A channel message can include optional fields that provide extra context, but only if its message type allows them. A length field tells the receiver how many octets of extra data follow.

sections.title: The G-ACh Label on Paths and Sections
sections.content:
An LSP or section needs a way to signal that its payload is a control message rather than user data. RFC 5586 assigns reserved MPLS label value 13 as the G-ACh Label (GAL). The GAL marks a G-ACh packet and indicates that the ACH follows the bottom of the label stack.

For MPLS-TP, the GAL is used on LSPs, concatenated segments and sections, not pseudowires, and it sits at the bottom of the label stack. A GAL must not appear in a normal user packet or more than once. The sending router places the message, optional TLVs and ACH behind the GAL and path label; intermediate routers must not modify them or forward the packet based on the GAL.

On a section, the GAL may be the only label, carrying a control message across the link between two routers. The GAL Time To Live must be at least 1; its exact value and Traffic Class setting depend on the application.
sections.plainLanguage: Label 13 tells a router that an MPLS payload contains a control message and that the ACH follows the end of the label stack. Intermediate routers leave the message intact, and the destination passes it to the right processing function.

sections.title: Existing Alerts and Unknown Channel Types
sections.content:
Existing IP-based MPLS OAM mechanisms, including TTL expiration and special IP destinations, remain the default when the OAM packet is carried in IP. RFC 5586 recommends the GAL mechanism when IP-based identification is unavailable, and it may also be used alongside those mechanisms.

RFC 3429 assigned label 14 as the OAM Alert Label. RFC 5586 uses a different label because G-ACh messages have a different position and broader set of maintenance uses, while existing systems already use label 14. A router must discard a received associated-channel packet when it cannot process or has not agreed to process the Channel Type, when an experimental type is disabled, or when the ACH marker or version is unrecognized.
sections.plainLanguage: The GAL adds a label-based option while older IP-based alert methods remain available. A router discards a control message if it cannot recognize or is not prepared to process its type.

sections.title: Security and Congestion
sections.content:
RFC 5586 refers security considerations for the ACH to RFC 4385. It also says the data-plane security considerations in RFC 5085 apply to G-ACh packets, whether they use the GAL or only the ACH.

Any additional security requirements belong in the specification for the relevant Channel Type. Congestion considerations from RFC 5085 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: This document relies on earlier RFCs for general security and congestion guidance. A specification for a new message type must describe any additional security requirements.

sections.title: Channel Type Registries
sections.content:
IANA assigned label value 13 to the GAL. Channel Types use the PW Associated Channel Type registry. Values 0 through 32751 use IETF Review, while values 32760 through 32767 are reserved for experiments.

Experimental functions must be disabled by default, and their Channel Type value must be configurable. The registry records whether an ACH TLV Header follows the ACH. RFC 5586 also creates an ACH TLV registry with IETF Review as its allocation policy and no initial entries.
sections.plainLanguage: Official registries assign the label and message-type values used by the channel. Experimental types must remain disabled until configured, helping avoid accidental use in normal operation.
